text: The framework I like to use with product leaders that I'm coaching is to think about a matrix.
speaker: Ravi Mehta
context: Lenny asks Ravi about his approach to product leadership and management. Ravi explains his framework for leading product teams, distinguishing between two effective leadership styles. He advocates for "selective micromanagement" as a temporary, tactical approach when teams need direction, rather than being completely hands-off when unsure about team direction.
text_ko: 제가 코칭하는 제품 리더분들과 함께 주로 쓰는 프레임워크(framework)는 매트릭스(matrix)로 생각하는 방식이에요.
text_zh: 我在辅导产品负责人（product leaders）时常用的一个框架，就是把事情放到一个矩阵里来思考。
text_es: Con los líderes de producto que asesoro (coaching), me gusta plantearlo como una matriz.
original_text: The framework I like to use with product leaders that I'm coaching is to think about a matrix. Your ideal goal is to lead in a scalable way, which means you feel really confident about the direction of your team and your team has the autonomy to move in that direction. There's another really effective way of leading, which is selective micromanagement, which if you don't feel confident in the direction that your team is moving, the right answer is not to be hands-off and to let them go in that wrong direction.

vocabulary.definition: A structured approach or system that provides guidance and support for understanding and addressing complex issues.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, a framework often refers to a set of principles or guidelines that help teams develop strategies, products, or processes effectively.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'framework' suggests a supportive structure, it can imply rigidity; thus, it is important to balance adherence to the framework with flexibility to adapt to changing circumstances.

vocabulary.definition: A two-dimensional array or grid used to organize and analyze data or relationships between different variables.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, a matrix can be utilized for decision-making, project management, or resource allocation, allowing for a more comprehensive view of interdependencies.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'matrix' can imply complexity and interconnectedness; it is often used when discussing multifaceted problems or organizational structures.

vocabulary.definition: A developmental process in which an individual provides support, feedback, and guidance to help another person improve their skills or performance.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the workplace, coaching is used to enhance employee performance, develop leadership skills, and foster professional growth through personalized feedback and goal-setting.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'coaching' implies a collaborative and supportive relationship, distinguishing it from more directive forms of training or mentoring.

text: There's this common, I would say it's a misconception that startups are faster than larger companies. And what I found initially is actually things felt slower when I started my own company because I didn't have as many engineers to work with.
speaker: Ravi Mehta
context: Lenny asks Ravi about the biggest differences between being a product leader at a big company versus starting his own company. Ravi explains a counterintuitive insight about startup speed, distinguishing between velocity (quantity of work) and latency (time from idea to testing). He uses this to explain why startups have advantages in agility rather than raw output.
text_ko: 사람들이 흔히 ‘스타트업(startup)이 대기업(large companies)보다 더 빠르다’고 하는데, 저는 그게 오해라고 봐요. 제가 직접 회사를 시작했을 때 처음 느낀 건 오히려 일이 더 느리게 느껴졌다는 거예요. 같이 일할 엔지니어(engineers)가 많지 않았거든요.
text_zh: 有个普遍的误解，大家觉得初创公司(startups)比大公司动作更快。但我自己刚创办公司的时候，反而觉得事情推进得更慢——因为工程师(engineers)不够多。
text_es: Hay una idea muy extendida, diría que equivocada, de que las startups son más rápidas que las empresas grandes. Y lo que descubrí al principio fue que, en realidad, todo iba más despacio cuando monté mi propia empresa, porque no tenía tantos ingenieros con los que contar.
key_sentence: The misconception is that startups are faster than larger companies.
original_text: There's this common, I would say it's a misconception that startups are faster than larger companies. And what I found initially is actually things felt slower when I started my own company because I didn't have as many engineers to work with. The advantage a smaller company has really is in latency. You can have an idea one day, you can test it the next day, and as a result you can have this really short cycle time between an assumption or a hypothesis and being able to validate that hypothesis.

vocabulary.definition: A misunderstanding or incorrect belief about a particular subject.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, misconceptions can lead to flawed strategies or decisions, particularly when assessing market dynamics or operational efficiencies.
vocabulary.nuance: While often used to address common errors in understanding, it can imply a need for clarification or education on the topic.

vocabulary.definition: Professionals who apply scientific and mathematical principles to design, develop, and maintain structures, systems, or processes.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech startups, engineers are crucial for product development and innovation, often driving the technical aspects of a company’s offerings.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply not just technical skills but also problem-solving abilities and creativity in addressing complex challenges.

text: I've had to shift my mindset from an experimental-oriented approach to making decisions to much more of a conviction-oriented approach.
speaker: Ravi Mehta
context: Ravi continues explaining differences between big companies and startups, focusing on decision-making approaches. He describes how startups can't rely on experimental approaches due to limited user bases for statistical significance, requiring instead a conviction-based approach where you gather enough data to make informed decisions quickly rather than getting stuck in analysis paralysis.
text_ko: 의사결정을 할 때 실험 중심 접근(experimental-oriented approach)에서 훨씬 더 신념 중심 접근(conviction-oriented approach)으로 마인드셋을 바꿔야 했어요.
text_zh: 我不得不把做决策的方式，从以实验为主 (experimental-oriented) 转为更以信念为主 (conviction-oriented)。
text_es: He tenido que pasar de tomar decisiones basadas en la experimentación a tomarlas más por convicción.
key_sentence: shift my mindset from an experimental-oriented approach to making decisions to much more of a conviction-oriented approach.
original_text: I've had to shift my mindset from an experimental-oriented approach to making decisions to much more of a conviction-oriented approach. And I've often found myself asking the question of like, do we just have enough data to have informed conviction and we should move forward and stop digging, move forward in a particular direction, and then see whether or not that turns out to be the right one?

vocabulary.definition: A mindset is a set of beliefs or attitudes that shape how an individual perceives and reacts to situations. It influences decision-making and behavior in various contexts.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a growth mindset can drive innovation and adaptability, while a fixed mindset may hinder progress and responsiveness to change.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies a deep-seated perspective that can be challenging to alter, making it crucial to recognize when a shift in mindset is necessary.

vocabulary.definition: An experimental-oriented approach emphasizes testing hypotheses and exploring new ideas through trial and error. It focuses on learning from outcomes to refine strategies.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups, an experimental-oriented mindset is vital for innovation, allowing teams to iterate on products and services based on user feedback and market response.
vocabulary.nuance: While beneficial for fostering creativity, this approach may lead to indecision if not balanced with concrete goals and timelines.

vocabulary.definition: A conviction-oriented approach is characterized by strong beliefs and principles that guide decision-making, often prioritizing values over empirical evidence. It reflects a commitment to a particular vision or strategy.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business leadership, being conviction-oriented can inspire teams and stakeholders, but it may also lead to resistance against alternative viewpoints or data-driven insights.
vocabulary.nuance: This term suggests a level of confidence that can be motivating, but it risks becoming inflexible if not tempered with openness to new information.

text: The analogy I like to use, it's a little bit like working with an architect.
speaker: Ravi Mehta
context: Lenny asks Ravi about his belief that product visions should be visual rather than just written documents. Ravi explains why wireframes are essential in strategy documents, using an architect analogy to illustrate how visual representations create better alignment than words alone. He argues that since products are ultimately visual (pixels on screen), strategy should include visual elements.
text_ko: 제가 즐겨 쓰는 비유가 하나 있는데, 건축가와 함께 일하는 것과 비슷해요.
text_zh: 我常打个比方：这有点像跟建筑师合作。
text_es: La comparación que me gusta hacer es pensar en esto como trabajar con un arquitecto.
key_sentence: it's a little bit like working with an architect.
original_text: The analogy I like to use, it's a little bit like working with an architect. You would never work with an architect that didn't provide you a blueprint of the house that they want to build for you because being able to describe a house in words alone is not enough. Everyone will come away from that with sort of a different interpretation of what is needed.

vocabulary.definition: A comparison between two different things that highlights some form of similarity, often used to explain complex concepts through familiar terms.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, analogies are frequently employed in presentations and discussions to simplify complex ideas, making them more relatable to stakeholders or team members.
vocabulary.nuance: While analogies can enhance understanding, they should be used carefully to avoid oversimplification or misinterpretation of the subject matter.

vocabulary.definition: A professional who designs and plans the construction of buildings and other structures, often requiring a blend of creativity and technical knowledge.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, the term 'architect' can also refer to someone who designs systems or strategies, such as a software architect who outlines the architecture of software applications.
vocabulary.nuance: The term carries a connotation of expertise and authority, suggesting a high level of skill in both design and execution, and should be used to denote someone with significant experience.

text: Ultimately, a PM needs to measure their success based on whether or not they generate valuable outcomes for the business.
speaker: Ravi Mehta
context: Lenny asks Ravi about his insights on goal-setting and best practices for aligning on goals. Ravi discusses problems with the common "outcomes over outputs" mantra, explaining that while ultimately PMs should drive business outcomes, it doesn't mean every quarter should have outcome-based commitments, especially when teams don't understand how to move those metrics.
text_ko: 궁극적으로 프로덕트 매니저(Product Manager)는 비즈니스에 실제로 가치 있는 결과를 만들어냈는지로 자신의 성공을 측정해야 해요.
text_zh: 说到底，作为产品经理(PM)，判断自己是否成功，关键在于有没有为业务带来真正有价值的成果。
text_es: Al final del día, un responsable de producto (PM) tiene que medir su éxito en función de si genera resultados que aporten valor al negocio.
key_sentence: Ultimately, a PM needs to measure their success based on whether or not they generate valuable outcomes for the business.
original_text: One of the things that I found, which I think was sort of a first principle that's happening at a lot of companies, is this idea of always focusing on outcomes over outputs and comes from a good place, which is ultimately, and I think this is the case, ultimately, a PM needs to measure their success based on whether or not they generate valuable outcomes for the business. But that doesn't necessarily mean that in this quarter we need to commit to a specific outcome or that we should commit to a specific outcome that we may or may not know how to move.

vocabulary.definition: To assess the size, amount, or degree of something using a standard unit.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, measuring success often involves quantifying performance metrics such as revenue growth, customer satisfaction, or project completion rates.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'measure' is often used in a quantitative sense, it can also imply a qualitative assessment in certain contexts.

vocabulary.definition: Results or consequences that provide significant benefits or advantages to an organization.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, valuable outcomes are often tied to strategic objectives, such as increased profitability, enhanced customer loyalty, or improved operational efficiency.
vocabulary.nuance: The term emphasizes the importance of not just achieving results, but ensuring those results contribute meaningfully to the organization's goals.

text: And so one of the things that we said with stake that we put in the ground was the strategy doc wouldn't be complete without wireframes. This was the first time that we were doing that in the context of strategy.
speaker: Ravi Mehta
context: Ravi shares an example from his time at Tripadvisor when they were developing a strategy for trip planning features. He explains how they established a rule requiring wireframes in strategy documents to create better alignment. This was an innovative approach at the time, designed to prevent different interpretations of written strategy by making the vision visually concrete.
text_ko: 그래서 우리가 확고히 정해 둔 것 중 하나는 전략 문서(strategy doc)가 와이어프레임(wireframes) 없이 완전하지 않다는 거였어요. 그리고 이런 식으로 전략의 맥락에서 와이어프레임을 포함한 건 이번이 처음이었어요.
text_zh: 所以我们当时就定下规矩：没有线框图 (wireframes)，战略文档 (strategy doc) 就不算完整。这是我们第一次在战略层面把线框图也纳进来。
text_es: Una de las cosas en las que nos comprometimos fue que el documento de estrategia no estaría completo sin las maquetas (wireframes). Era la primera vez que hacíamos eso en el contexto de la estrategia.
key_sentence: the strategy doc wouldn't be complete without wireframes.
original_text: And so one of the things that we said with stake that we put in the ground was the strategy doc wouldn't be complete without wireframes. This was the first time that we were doing that in the context of strategy. And the thing that we were really trying to solve for is the fact that oftentimes when you talk about strategy in words alone, everyone takes away a different interpretation of that strategy, whereas when you actually can show people wireframes of what the product will look like when that strategy is implemented, it creates much more alignment.

vocabulary.definition: A plan of action designed to achieve a long-term or overall aim. It involves the allocation of resources and the prioritization of goals.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, strategy refers to the comprehensive approach taken to position a company in the market, often involving competitive analysis and resource management.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'strategy' implies a well-thought-out plan, it can sometimes suggest rigidity; flexibility in execution is often necessary.

vocabulary.definition: The circumstances or setting surrounding an event, statement, or idea that help to clarify its meaning. It provides the background necessary for understanding.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, context is crucial for interpreting data, decisions, or strategies, as it shapes the relevance and implications of the information presented.
vocabulary.nuance: Context can imply a broader perspective, and neglecting it may lead to misinterpretations or oversights.
